A review-specific cataract artificial intelligence clinical continuum (CAICC) evidence-mapping framework was developed during data charting and synthesis. Two reviewers independently conducted study selection, data extraction, endpoint adjudication, and validation-maturity assessment. Performance was summarized descriptively; validation maturity characterized evaluation independence and clinical stage, not risk of bias or overall methodological quality.

Results

Of 361 reports sought for retrieval, 122 (33.8%) were not retrieved; 113/122 (92.6%) were considered plausibly eligible from available metadata. The final synthesis included 185 studies: detection (n = 52), characterization (n = 50), personalized surgical planning (n = 27), intelligent surgery (n = 28), recovery (n = 24), and patient engagement (n = 4). Among 181 validation-applicable included studies, internal testing was the most frequent highest-maturity category (123/181, 68.0%), followed by external testing (33/181, 18.2%), prospective single-center evaluation (6/181, 3.3%), and prospective multicenter evaluation (2/181, 1.1%); 17/181 (9.4%) had no independent or unclear testing. Among the retrieved and included studies, no comprehensive clinically validated multimodal preoperative cataract surgical-complexity model was identified.

Conclusions

Most included studies remained at internal validation stages, and prospective multicenter evaluation was rare. Because 122/361 reports sought for retrieval were unavailable and most were considered plausibly eligible, retrieval bias may affect the comprehensiveness of the evidence map. Future research should prioritize multimodal preoperative surgical-complexity prediction, independent external testing, and prospective multicenter evaluation of locked models.

Registration

Open Science Framework (OSF), DOI 10.17605/OSF.IO/ZKM86.

records.title: Smartphone-Based Deep Learning Exophthalmometry in Thyroid Eye Disease: A Multicenter, Multiethnic Validation Study.
records.publisher: Thyroid : official journal of the American Thyroid Association

content.title: Smartphone-Based Deep Learning Exophthalmometry in Thyroid Eye Disease: A Multicenter, Multiethnic Validation Study.
content.abstract:
Background

Proptosis is the principal quantitative measure of disease severity in thyroid eye disease (TED), but Hertel exophthalmometry has substantial interobserver variability and requires in-person specialist visits. Existing deep learning (DL) proptosis-from-photograph models require studio-acquired images. We aimed to validate, in a multicenter multiethnic study, a DL model fine-tuned to estimate proptosis (mm) from nonstudio facial photographs-smartphone selfies or clinician-taken photographs.

Methods

This validation study included 361 patients with confirmed or suspected TED at three institutions. Data were collected prospectively at two Korean sites-Severance Hospital (SH; 203 patients/3654 facial images; internal validation) and Seoul National University Bundang Hospital (SNUBH; 79/933; same-ethnicity external validation)-and retrospectively, from routine-care images, at one Spanish site, Virgen Macarena University Hospital (HUVM; 79/336; different-ethnicity external validation). Korean patients self-acquired selfies on six smartphone models per site using a capture-guidance application; Spanish images were clinician-acquired during routine care without such guidance. The model-a dual-stream ResNet-18 jointly processing a facial image and a per-pixel depth map (ZoeDepth)-outputs a proptosis estimate (mm) per eye from one photograph and was fine-tuned, from a previously published model trained on studio digital single-lens reflex photographs, for these nonstudio acquisitions. Hertel measurements by oculoplastic specialists served as the reference standard.

Results

On single-image analysis, the mean absolute error (MAE) versus Hertel measurement was 1.14 mm (Pearson correlation coefficient [PCC] 0.83) in SH, 1.44 mm (PCC 0.85) in SNUBH, and 1.58 mm (PCC 0.77) in HUVM, with predictions within 2 mm of Hertel in 83.6%, 71.3%, and 69.7% of images, respectively. Performance was consistent across 12 smartphone models (per-device MAE 1.11-1.54 mm). For detecting severe proptosis (Hertel ≥21 mm), the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve was 0.94 (confidence interval 0.93-0.96), 0.91 (0.89-0.92), and 0.86 (0.82-0.91) in SH, SNUBH, and HUVM, respectively. Bland-Altman analysis revealed underestimation at the upper extreme.

Conclusions

An artificial intelligence model fine-tuned for nonstudio facial photographs achieved Hertel-level agreement and reliable severity discrimination across 2 ethnicities and 12 smartphones, both for patient self-acquired smartphone selfies and for clinician-acquired routine clinic photographs, providing a scalable approach for patient-facing and clinic-based monitoring of TED severity, pending further longitudinal validation.

records.title: Retinal Artificial Intelligence Reclassifies SCORE2-Based Cardiovascular Risk Across the ESC/EAS Statin-Indication Boundary: A UK Biobank Prospective Cohort Study.

content.title: Retinal Artificial Intelligence Reclassifies SCORE2-Based Cardiovascular Risk Across the ESC/EAS Statin-Indication Boundary: A UK Biobank Prospective Cohort Study.
content.abstract:
Aims

Whether a retinal artificial intelligence (AI) risk score reclassifies SCORE2 cardiovascular risk stratification in statin-naive adults across the ESC/EAS statin-indication boundary is uncertain. We evaluated the retinal AI risk score for 10-year atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD) prediction.

Methods

In 40,672 statin-naive UK Biobank participants (aged 40-69, without diabetes), cardiovascular risk categories and treatment recommendation status (Class I or IIa vs neither) were defined using the 2025 ESC/EAS focused-update framework. Cox models estimated hazard ratios (HRs) adjusted for SCORE2 or for established risk factors. The incremental predictive value of adding the retinal AI risk score to SCORE2 was evaluated using 10-fold cross-validation.

Results

Over a 10.0-year median follow-up (914 ASCVD events), the very high retinal AI risk group independently predicted ASCVD (SCORE2-adjusted HR 2.32 vs low risk; p<0.001). Adding the retinal AI risk score to SCORE2 reclassified risk across the ESC/EAS statin-indication boundary (statin-eligibility NRI [net reclassification improvement] 0.012, p<0.001); reclassification was statistically significant but modest (continuous NRI 0.445, p<0.001), without C-index or net-benefit gain. In the statin-indicated subgroup, retinal AI risk groups further stratified risk (SCORE2-adjusted HR 2.16; p<0.001). Statin-not-indicated participants in the high or very high retinal AI risk groups had numerically similar observed 10-year risk to all statin-indicated, untreated participants (p=0.758). There was no evidence of effect modification by clinically detectable retinal disorder (interaction p=0.93). Incremental value was greater in women than men (sex interaction p<0.001).

Conclusion

Adding the retinal AI risk score to SCORE2 produced modest bidirectional risk reclassification across the ESC/EAS statin-indication boundary; these findings warrant prospective validation.Abstract word count: 250 words.

records.title: The Duke Clinically Linked Electrocardiogram and Arrhythmia Repository.

content.title: The Duke Clinically Linked Electrocardiogram and Arrhythmia Repository.
content.abstract: Artificial intelligence-electrocardiogram (ECG) algorithms are becoming increasingly powerful tools in the clinical world, allowing for earlier and subclinical detection of ubiquitous and harmful pathologies. However, the strength of these algorithms is directly informed by the strength of the data sets on which they are trained, and there is a growing need for large-scale, diverse, publicly available ECG repositories. The Duke Clinically Linked ECG and Arrhythmia Repository is a large-scale ECG database containing over 5 million clinically acquired ECGs linked to longitudinal clinical data. Its strengths-including demographic diversity, large sample size, linked clinical databases, breadth of represented conditions, access to linked procedure codes, various options for data export, and ease in creating targeted subcohorts-position it as a significant tool in the artificial intelligence-ECG research landscape. This Methods paper outlines the demographics and structure of this database and explores promising research applications of this resource.

records.title: Automated Structured Reporting of Neurodegenerative Imaging Markers Using Quantitative MRI and Large Language Models.

content.title: Automated Structured Reporting of Neurodegenerative Imaging Markers Using Quantitative MRI and Large Language Models.
content.abstract:
Rationale and objectives

To evaluate the feasibility of a quantitative magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)-to-structured reporting pipeline that integrates quantitative MRI software with large language models (LLMs) for structured drafting of neurodegenerative imaging markers and generating clinician-facing report conclusions.

Materials and methods

A total of 192 patients with 3D T1 and 2D or 3D FLAIR MRI images from the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative database were randomly selected. A deep-learning model generated structured report findings based on nine indices related to brain atrophy, white matter hyperintensities, and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) space abnormalities, and compared with neuroradiologist-generated reference reports. Four LLMs (GPT-OSS 20B, MedGemma 4B, Phi-3, and Llama 3.1 8B) generated clinician-facing conclusions from the structured findings. Generated conclusions were evaluated using a five-point Likert scale across four metrics (accuracy, relevance, clarity, and satisfaction). Output errors were assessed across four categories: language, omission, addition, and numeric errors.

Results

Structured report findings demonstrated high accuracy for CSF space analysis (77.6%-97.9%). Performance for ordinal visual scales was lower under strict matching (27.1%-57.8%) but improved with a one-grade tolerance (91.7%-97.4%). Among LLMs, GPT achieved the highest scores across most metrics (median score 5) and exhibited the lowest output error rates. Smaller models (Phi-3 and Llama 3.1 8B) showed overall lower performance, with more language, omission, and addition errors. MedGemma demonstrated intermediate performance, but the highest rate of numeric errors.

Conclusion

Our quantitative MRI-to-structured reporting pipeline, integrating quantitative MRI software with LLM-based conclusion generation, might be feasible for automated structured drafting of neurodegenerative imaging markers.

records.title: Histopathological Imaging and Artificial Intelligence for Cancer Diagnosis and Gleason Grading: A Brief Review of Prostate Cancer.
records.publisher: Journal of clinical practice and research

content.title: Histopathological Imaging and Artificial Intelligence for Cancer Diagnosis and Gleason Grading: A Brief Review of Prostate Cancer.
content.abstract:
Objective

Prostate cancer, one of the most common cancers affecting men's health worldwide, ranks second among cancer-related deaths. Therefore, it represents a critical health issue, and early diagnosis is crucial. Several imaging and analytical methods are used to diagnose this condition.

Materials and methods

This study focuses on research conducted between 2021 and 2025 that analyzes, diagnoses, and grades prostate cancer based on histopathological images using machine learning and deep learning algorithms. In this context, the reviewed studies also include an analysis of findings related to preprocessing and feature extraction methods that may aid in prostate cancer detection, as well as the classifiers used.

Results

According to the findings of the reviewed studies, artificial intelligence-supported prostate cancer detection systems demonstrate high clinical performance and significantly improve the diagnostic accuracy of pathologists by enabling rapid diagnosis. The presented research findings indicate a need for comprehensive studies focusing on prostate cancer using histopathological images.

Conclusion

The integration of artificial intelligence is transforming prostate cancer pathology from a traditional and subjective process into a data-driven and standardized framework. This systematic analysis of histopathological images will make significant contributions to future prostate cancer research, help achieve more reliable results in clinical decision-making processes, and lay the groundwork for personalized medicine.

records.title: Accuracy and reproducibility of a large language model in assessing spirometry test acceptability and interpretation: a performance study.

content.title: Accuracy and reproducibility of a large language model in assessing spirometry test acceptability and interpretation: a performance study.
content.abstract:
Background

Spirometry is one of the most used pulmonary function tests for assessing respiratory function and diagnosing ventilatory disorders in clinical practice. Evaluation of test validity and interpretation is typically performed by trained healthcare professionals. The present study aims to evaluate the capability of a publicly available large language model (LLM) to perform quality assurance and interpretations of spirometry tests.

Methods

A total of 150 spirometry tests were retrospectively collected from the pulmonary function laboratories. The spirometry tests were evaluated for acceptability and interpreted by clinicians according to ATS/ERS recommendations as part of standard clinical practice. Subsequently, a publicly available LLM (ChatGPT 5.5) was prompted to evaluate the acceptability and interpret the same spirometry tests according to ATS/ERS criteria. The model interpreted each spirometry test on three separate occasions for assessing reproducibility. Accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value (PPV), and negative predictive value (NPV), with 95% confidence intervals (CIs), were calculated by comparing LLM assessments with clinician assessments of spirometry test acceptability and interpretation.

Results

For spirometry acceptability evaluation, ChatGPT demonstrated an overall accuracy of 87% (95% CI: 81%-92%), sensitivity of 91% (95% CI: 85%-95%), specificity of 61% (95% CI 39%-80%), PPV of 94% (95% CI: 89%-97%), and NPV of 48(95% CI: 29%-67%) with Cohen's k of 0.46. The spiromteric interpretation agreement with the clinicians reference standard was moderate, with exact agreement of 0.61 (95% CI: 0.54-0.69) while Cohen's Kappa (Unweighted) was 0.47 (95% CI: 0.37-0.56) and Macro F1 score was 0.39 (95% CI: 0.33-0.49). Reproducibility across three independent trials was moderate (Fleiss' κ 0.58). Class-specific interpretation performance varied by category; sensitivity was highest for normal pattern and restrictive defects (0.72), whereas sensitivity for obstructive defects was 0.27. F1-scores were highest for normal and restrictive defects (0.81 and 0.62, respectively).

Conclusion

The current findings suggest that ChatGPT 5.5 has a limited capability, at its current stage of development, to serve as a reliable tool for independent spirometry interpretation in clinical practice. Nevertheless, it may serve as an adjunct to clinical decision-making and educational tools. Prospective controlled studies are needed to confirm these findings.

records.title: Empirical Evaluation of Post Hoc Interpretability Methods for Clinical Trust in Deep Learning Diagnostics.

content.title: Empirical Evaluation of Post Hoc Interpretability Methods for Clinical Trust in Deep Learning Diagnostics.
content.abstract: Background/Objectives: Brain tumor classification from magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) has been significantly improved through deep learning techniques; however, the lack of interpretability remains a major challenge for clinical adoption. Methods: This study proposes an explainable artificial intelligence (XAI)-driven framework for multiclass brain tumor classification using a baseline convolutional neural network (CNN) and four transfer learning models, namely ResNet50, DenseNet121, MobileNetV2, and EfficientNetB0. The models were trained and evaluated on a publicly available brain MRI dataset consisting of glioma, meningioma, and pituitary tumor classes. Their classification performance was assessed using accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score, receiver operating characteristic area under the curve (ROC-AUC), and confusion matrix analysis. To enhance transparency and interpretability, Grad-CAM, LIME, and SHAP were used to visualize and quantify the regions contributing to the classification decisions. Results: Experimental results state that the transfer learning models consistently outperformed the CNN by learning more discriminative feature representations while producing more localized and interpretable explanations. The agreement among Grad-CAM, LIME, and SHAP confirms that the proposed models predominantly relied on tumor regions rather than irrelevant background information, thereby improving the interpretability and reliability of the diagnostic predictions. Conclusions: The proposed framework provides an effective and explainable computer-aided diagnosis system that supports trustworthy deep learning-based brain tumor classification and has the potential for decision-making.

records.title: Artificial intelligence, explainable deep learning, and generative models for osteoporosis and bone disease prediction: a systematic review and future research roadmap.

content.title: Artificial intelligence, explainable deep learning, and generative models for osteoporosis and bone disease prediction: a systematic review and future research roadmap.
content.abstract: Osteoporosis is a major global health burden, with considerable morbidity, mortality, and healthcare costs. Artificial intelligence (AI) has opened new avenues for osteoporosis screening, bone mineral density quantification, fracture-risk prediction, and clinical decision support, but progress remains fragmented across machine learning, deep learning, explainable AI (XAI), generative models, and multimodal learning. This systematic review brings these strands together and identifies priority research needs for AI-based osteoporosis prediction. Following the PRISMA 2020 statement, studies were identified from Scopus and Google Scholar, published between January 2020 and the final search date of 30 June 2026, with two reviewers screening independently and resolving disagreements by consensus. Design-related risk-of-bias indicators, such as retrospective vs. prospective design, validation strategy, and reference standard, were recorded for every study; a full PROBAST, QUADAS-2, and Newcastle-Ottawa Scale appraisal is planned but not yet complete. Fifty-eight studies met the inclusion criteria and were synthesized narratively and descriptively, without formal meta-analysis, given substantial heterogeneity. Findings spanned five themes: classical machine learning, deep learning for imaging, explainable AI, generative models, and multimodal learning. Deep learning achieved strong predictive accuracy (AUC 0.82-0.96), XAI improved clinical interpretability, generative models helped offset data scarcity, and multimodal approaches boosted performance by combining imaging and clinical data. Key gaps remain, including limited external validation, heavy reliance on retrospective data, poor generalisability, and limited regulatory readiness. Building on these findings, this review proposes MXGNet, a multimodal, explainable, generative framework incorporating privacy-preserving federated learning, intended to guide development of robust, interpretable, clinically deployable AI tools for osteoporosis prediction.

records.title: Artificial intelligence in image-guided cervical interventional radiotherapy: a systematic review.

content.title: Artificial intelligence in image-guided cervical interventional radiotherapy: a systematic review.
content.abstract:
Background

Imaging-guided interventional radiotherapy (IG-IRT) is the standard of care for locally advanced cervical cancer but remains time-consuming and operator-dependent. Artificial intelligence (AI) has emerged as a promising tool to improve efficiency and reproducibility.

Methods

A systematic review was conducted according to PRISMA 2020 guidelines, searching PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science for studies published between 2010 and 2026 investigating AI-based imaging applications in cervical IRT. Eligible studies included original research evaluating segmentation (targets and organ at risk), planning, reconstruction, image registration and applicator selection.

Results

Fifty-two studies were included. Deep learning-based segmentation showed variable performance across anatomical structures and studies, with Dice coefficients approaching or exceeding 0.90 for some organs at risk and target volumes in the best-performing models. Individual studies reported shorter processing times, reduced contouring variability, accurate applicator reconstruction, and potential support for applicator selection. However, the substantial methodological and clinical heterogeneity precluded direct comparisons among AI approaches.

Conclusions

The available studies suggest that AI may support the automation of selected workflow steps and assist treatment-related decision-making in image-guided cervical interventional radiotherapy. While several applications have achieved high technical performance, most remain at the proof-of-concept stage, and robust external validation and prospective clinical evaluation are needed before routine clinical adoption.

records.title: Artificial Intelligence in Breast Cancer Diagnosis, Treatment, and Perioperative Management: A Systematic Review of Current Applications and Future Perspectives.

content.title: Artificial Intelligence in Breast Cancer Diagnosis, Treatment, and Perioperative Management: A Systematic Review of Current Applications and Future Perspectives.
content.abstract:
Background

Breast cancer is the most frequently diagnosed malignancy in women globally, accounting for approximately 2.30 million new cases and 666,103 deaths in 2022. Artificial intelligence technologies including machine learning, deep learning, radiomics, and natural language processing have been widely applied across the breast cancer care continuum. However, no systematic review restricted to primary studies with patient-level or image-level data has synthesized evidence spanning all clinical domains simultaneously.

Objectives

To evaluate the performance, methodological quality, and clinical relevance of artificial intelligence primary studies across screening and diagnostic imaging, digital pathology, radiomics, perioperative management, prognostic prediction, and natural language processing in breast cancer.

Methods

PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, Web of Science, Embase, and the Cochrane Library were searched from January 2015 to May 2026. Eligibility was restricted to original primary research reporting patient-level or image-level data; secondary syntheses were explicitly excluded. Risk of bias was assessed using QUADAS-2 and PROBAST. Reporting followed PRISMA 2020 guidelines.

Results

Of 5,275 identified records, 17 primary studies met eligibility criteria. In screening mammography (seven studies; n = 7,540 to 144,231 examinations), deep learning achieved area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) values of 0.876 to 0.939; a randomised trial in 80,033 women demonstrated non-inferiority to double reading with a 44.3% reduction in radiologist workload. In digital pathology (five studies; 270 to 44,732 whole-slide images), deep learning achieved AUC 0.985 to 0.994, exceeding unassisted pathologist performance in lymph node metastasis detection. Magnetic resonance imaging radiomics predicted pathological complete response in HER2-positive breast cancer with AUC 0.80. No breast cancer-specific perioperative primary study met the eligibility criteria. Deep survival networks achieved concordance index 0.626 versus 0.612 for Cox regression in breast cancer cohorts. Natural language processing identified metastatic recurrence in breast cancer clinical records with sensitivity 83% and specificity 73%. Risk of bias was low to moderate for imaging and pathology studies and high for small sample radiomics studies. Density-stratified performance was reported by only two imaging studies, and receptor status prediction from haematoxylin and eosin staining had not been validated as a safe alternative to immunohistochemistry.

Conclusions

Artificial intelligence demonstrated clinically meaningful performance across the five domains with eligible primary studies. Breast cancer-specific perioperative and intensive care primary studies were absent, representing the largest evidence gap. External validation, demographic diversity, and prospective clinical integration evidence remained the most consistently identified limitations. Prediction of molecular receptor status without immunohistochemistry requires rigorous prospective safety validation before it can complement standard testing.

records.title: Is Large Language Model a New Hope for the Global South? A Rapid Bibliometric Synthesis of Artificial Intelligence in Anatomy Education.

content.title: Is Large Language Model a New Hope for the Global South? A Rapid Bibliometric Synthesis of Artificial Intelligence in Anatomy Education.
content.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI), especially the recent proliferation of generative Large Language Models (LLMs), is transforming traditional anatomy education by introducing new teaching tools. However, the adoption of these cutting-edge technologies raises questions about global educational equity. It remains unclear whether AI will serve as a digital equalizer or further exacerbate marginalization. This rapid bibliometric synthesis aims to provide a comprehensive, data-driven overview of the "Application of Artificial Intelligence in Anatomy Education" (AAAE). We seek to map the intellectual landscape, detect structural and technological shifts, evaluate the geopolitical disparities, and provide corresponding references. A total of 85 consolidated records were retrieved from Web of Science and Scopus. These data constituted the whole panorama of AAAE. Bibliometrix and CiteSpace were utilized for static and dynamic mapping. A multidisciplinary expert panel validated the thematic clusters using Gwet's AC1 and the Normalized Herfindahl-Hirschman Index (HHI). Publications surged following ChatGPT's release, indicating a shift from specialized computer vision to the application of general-purpose LLMs. While high-income countries maintain leadership, AI could exert a "democratizing effect" on upper-middle-income countries, doubling their odds of publication compared to traditional anatomy. Six research frontiers and three research trajectories were captured, and corresponding implications for future researchers in the global south and north were presented. AAAE could be conducted using a stratified strategy: different expansions of AI technologies for pedagogy; leveraging commercial APIs to bypass infrastructure bottlenecks; and validating open-source models. Global equity critically demands cross-border collaboration and inclusive datasets.

records.title: Artificial Intelligence, Machine Learning, and Deep Learning Approaches for Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder Diagnosis: Protocol for a Scoping Review.

content.title: Artificial Intelligence, Machine Learning, and Deep Learning Approaches for Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder Diagnosis: Protocol for a Scoping Review.
content.abstract:
Background

Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) affects over 366 million adults and 139 million children worldwide, yet diagnosis remains fundamentally subjective, relying on clinical interviews, behavioral observations, and rating scales that yield inconsistent results across practitioners and settings. Artificial intelligence (AI), machine learning (ML), and deep learning (DL) offer a paradigm shift toward objective, data-driven diagnosis by detecting complex patterns across neuroimaging, electrophysiology, and digital biomarkers that elude conventional assessment. Although AI-based ADHD research has grown exponentially, no comprehensive synthesis examines the full spectrum of data modalities, validation practices, and clinical translation readiness. This gap limits our understanding of which approaches are most promising for real-world implementation.

Objective

This scoping review will visually map the current evidence on AI-based ADHD classification with respect to predictive accuracy, data forms, data features, generalizability, and interpretability of models.

Methods

This scoping review will use the Joanna Briggs Institute approach to scoping reviews and follow the PRISMA-ScR (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses extension for Scoping Reviews) guidelines. Five electronic databases (IEEE Xplore, Scopus, PubMed, Web of Science, and ACM Digital Library) will be systematically searched for peer-reviewed studies published between January 2019 and April 2026. Empirical studies in English involving the use of AI, ML, DL, or explainable AI to diagnose ADHD with a total sample size greater than 100 participants (ADHD and control groups combined) and a non-ADHD control group (individuals with typical development or healthy individuals) will be included. Two independent reviewers will screen the titles, abstracts, and full texts, and any conflicts will be resolved through either discussion or arbitration. A standardized Microsoft Excel template will be used to extract data that will include the following: bibliographic data, data modalities, data models, data validation approaches, performance metrics, and explainability approaches. Thematic and narrative analysis will be used to synthesize findings on 4 research questions that will address model performance, data modality contributions, data characteristics, and interpretability methods.

Results

The scoping review began in December 2025. Analysis and screening are in progress, with the scoping review expected to be completed and submitted for publication in June 2026.

Conclusions

This scoping review will provide the first comprehensive synthesis of AI-, ML-, and DL-based ADHD diagnostic classification studies, mapping the evidence across data modalities, validation practices, interpretability methods, and clinical translation readiness. Findings will inform future methodological standards and support the translation of AI-based diagnostic tools into clinical practice.

records.title: The Influence of Large Language Model-Generated Artificial Intelligence Risk Estimates on Clinical Decision-Making in Breast Imaging: A Simulation-Based Study.

content.title: The Influence of Large Language Model-Generated Artificial Intelligence Risk Estimates on Clinical Decision-Making in Breast Imaging: A Simulation-Based Study.
content.abstract: Background/Objectives: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used as decision-support tools in radiology, yet their influence on clinical decision-making remains a significant concern. This study evaluates how artificial intelligence (AI)-generated malignancy risk estimates influence clinical decisions in breast imaging and assesses automation bias (AB) among radiology residents at different training levels. Methods: In this simulation-based study, 20 residents reviewed radiology reports for 15 synthetic breast imaging cases generated by ChatGPT-4 Turbo, each presented in either a concordant or discordant format. Participants were stratified into two groups based on their completion of a breast imaging rotation and evaluated each case by assigning a BI-RADS score, recommending management, and rating their confidence in the AI risk estimate. Diagnostic accuracy and independent predictors of AB were analyzed using Generalized Estimating Equations (GEE) to account for reader-level clustering. Results: Overall management accuracy was significantly lower in cases with discordant AI outputs (p = 0.008). A similar, albeit non-significant, decreasing trend was observed for BI-RADS accuracy. While advanced residents maintained high management accuracy regardless of AI concordance, early-stage residents showed a sharp decline in discordant cases (77.3% vs. 45.3%; p = 0.006). This decline was most critical in malignant cases for early-stage residents, where accuracy dropped from 92.0% to 48.0% (p < 0.001). In the multivariable GEE logistic regression model, training level was the only independent predictor of AB (OR: 0.09, 95% CI: 0.03-0.28, p < 0.001). Conclusions: In this simulation study, advanced clinical training was associated with lower susceptibility to AB in breast imaging, although training level alone is unlikely to be a sufficient safeguard. Safe integration of AI tools will require caution among junior trainees alongside system-level measures such as model transparency and institutional oversight.

records.title: Advancing Cancer Biomarker Discovery Through Multi-Omics, Bioinformatics, and Artificial Intelligence: A Systematic Review.

content.title: Advancing Cancer Biomarker Discovery Through Multi-Omics, Bioinformatics, and Artificial Intelligence: A Systematic Review.
content.abstract: The rapid accumulation of multi-omics data provides increasing opportunities for cancer biomarker discovery, but the heterogeneity and high dimensionality of these datasets remain major challenges for data integration and analysis. This review examines the application of bioinformatics and artificial intelligence for multi-omics integration in cancer biomarker research. Common multi-omics data paradigms and integration strategies are discussed, followed by a review of the bioinformatics, machine learning and deep learning approaches applied across 84 included studies. Cross-study comparison showed limited recurrence among the reported biomarkers, with only 15 biomarkers identified in at least four studies. Further assessment of the 13 recurrent protein-coding biomarkers showed significant protein-protein interaction enrichment and functional convergence in cancer-related processes, particularly PI3K/AKT and ERBB2-related signaling. This review also highlights current challenges, including missing data, heterogeneity across datasets, limited independent validation and the interpretability of artificial intelligence models. Future research may benefit from integrating multi-omics data with clinical information, pathological imaging, electronic health records, single-cell multi-omics and radiomics, together with broader datasets and greater use of independent validation to support the translation of multi-omics biomarker findings into clinical applications.

records.title: Comparative analysis and optimization of multi-model artificial intelligence for microscopic detection of fungal structures in superficial fungal infections.
records.publisher: Frontiers in cellular and infection microbiology

content.title: Comparative analysis and optimization of multi-model artificial intelligence for microscopic detection of fungal structures in superficial fungal infections.
content.abstract:
Background

Superficial fungal infections present a growing threat to global public health. Traditional diagnostic techniques, including microscopy and culture, are time-consuming and subjective, often limiting diagnostic accuracy. Artificial intelligence (AI)-driven diagnostic tools offer a promising adjunct to improve efficiency and standardization of microscopic fungal detection.

Methods

We systematically compared six deep learning models, including the You Only Look Once (YOLO) series, the Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) series and the Detection Transformer (DETR). Three evaluation datasets were constructed. Datasets 1 and 2 (derived from 4000 hyphae and 4500 spore images) were used to assess image-level detection using sensitivity, precision and F1 score. Dataset 1 was manually annotated for the YOLO series and DETR; Dataset 2 (unannotated) served as the CNN series' benchmark. Dataset 3 (1, 870 specimens from 1, 730 patients) was used to evaluate sample-level performance via confusion matrix analysis for the YOLO series and DETR models, employing medical records as the reference standard. The best-performing model was optimized and deployed into an online auxiliary diagnostic platform for real-time clinical decision support.

Results

YOLOv11 outperformed all other evaluated architectures. Detection was generally better at 400× than at 200× magnification. Notably, the F1 score for hyphae detection by YOLOv11 increased from 90.42% (200×) to 92.06% (400×). All models achieved higher accuracy for spores than hyphae. Patient-level confusion-matrix analysis confirmed YOLOv11 superiority. After optimizing an Intersection over Union (IoU) threshold of 0.25 and the maximum confidence (Cmax) strategy, 200× hyphae F1 rose to 97.84% and the positive predictive value (PPV) to 98.27%. Subgroup analysis showed robust performance across different diseases, with tinea capitis reaching the highest F1 score (98.53%).

Conclusion

The optimized YOLOv11 model demonstrates potential as a rapid and standardized supportive tool for the microscopic detection of fungal structures in superficial fungal infections. Integration into an online auxiliary diagnostic platform demonstrates the feasibility of real-time AI-assisted fungal detection, offering a standardized tool to support clinical decision-making. This work supports AI as a potential complement to clinical and laboratory expertise, pending further validation in prospective and multi-center settings, and highlights its potential to streamline fungal infection diagnostic workflows.

records.title: Experimental Protocols for Developing and Validating Explainable AI Models in Secure Healthcare Diagnostics.

content.title: Experimental Protocols for Developing and Validating Explainable AI Models in Secure Healthcare Diagnostics.
content.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) has drastically enhanced healthcare diagnostics with automated disease detection, predictive analytics, and intelligent systems for clinical decision support. Nevertheless, the black-box nature of deep learning models hampers interpretability, clinical trust, and regulatory acceptance and raises concerns about data privacy and cybersecurity. This paper presents comprehensive experimental frameworks for developing and evaluating explainable AI models for secure healthcare diagnostics. The suggested model combines responsible data management, multimodal preprocessing, secure deep learning models, explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) methods, and reproducible validation procedures in a single healthcare diagnostic pipeline. Methods of explaining, such as Grad-CAM, SHAP, LIME, and counterfactual analysis, were used to make the models more transparent and understandable for clinicians. At the same time, federated learning and differential privacy methods were used to securely manage highly sensitive patient data. Experimental evaluation has shown 96% classification accuracy, 94% sensitivity, and 95% specificity. These results were consistent in heterogeneous healthcare datasets. Compared to traditional black-box models, the explainability framework not only enhanced the interpretability of the results but also more accurately identified the regions relevant for diagnosis. Moreover, the secure federated learning architecture minimized privacy leakages without sacrificing the predictive performance and remained robust even when exposed to adversarial perturbations. An external evaluation also confirmed the reproducibility and generalizability of the protocols involved. This methodology offers a comprehensive and reliable foundation for deploying AI-powered diagnostics across multiple healthcare domains: radiology, pathology, oncology, cardiology, neurology, and precision medicine.

records.title: Diagnostic Accuracy of Artificial Intelligence for Detecting ST-Elevation Myocardial Infarction on 12-Lead Electrocardiograms: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.

content.title: Diagnostic Accuracy of Artificial Intelligence for Detecting ST-Elevation Myocardial Infarction on 12-Lead Electrocardiograms: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
content.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) may improve electrocardiographic detection of ST-elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI), but available studies address distinct diagnostic questions. We systematically reviewed studies evaluating AI-based STEMI detection from 12-lead electrocardiograms and separately synthesized AI performance against a clinical reference standard, AI and clinician performance against a clinical reference, and AI agreement with physician electrocardiogram (ECG) interpretation. PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, Scopus, Cochrane Library, and ClinicalTrials.gov were searched from January 2010 through March 10, 2025. Bivariate random-effects models generated pooled sensitivity, specificity, and hierarchical summary receiver operating characteristic area under the curve (AUC). Twenty-six studies comprising 539,876 ECGs were included. In 20 studies comparing AI with a clinical reference standard, pooled sensitivity was 0.95 (95% confidence interval, 0.91-0.97), specificity 0.95 (0.90-0.98), AUC 0.98 (0.97-0.99), positive likelihood ratio 19.2 (9.3-39.5), and negative likelihood ratio 0.05 (0.03-0.10). In 8 studies reporting both AI and clinician performance against a clinical reference, separate syntheses showed sensitivity of 0.91 (0.86-0.94) for AI versus 0.78 (0.69-0.85) for clinicians, specificity of 0.91 (0.82-0.96) for both, and AUCs of 0.95 and 0.90, respectively. In 7 studies using physician ECG interpretation as the comparator, AI sensitivity was 0.85 (0.70-0.94), specificity 0.99 (0.96-1.00), and AUC 0.98 (0.96-0.99). Sensitivity analyses excluding case-control designs, influential studies, and restricting analyses to deep learning models or raw waveform ECGs produced similar findings.

records.title: Computed tomography-based artificial intelligence for predicting preoperative microvascular invasion in hepatocellular carcinoma: a systematic review and meta-analysis.

content.title: Computed tomography-based artificial intelligence for predicting preoperative microvascular invasion in hepatocellular carcinoma: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
content.abstract:
Purpose

This meta-analysis evaluates the diagnostic performance of computed tomography (CT)-based artificial intelligence (AI) models versus radiologists for preoperative microvascular invasion (MVI) detection in hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC).

Methods

A systematic literature search was conducted in PubMed, Embase, and Web of Science to identify studies published up to February 2025 focusing on the diagnostic accuracy of CT-based AI models for the preoperative detection of MVI in HCC, compared with the diagnostic performance of radiologists. A bivariate random-effects model was employed to calculate the pooled sensitivity, specificity, and area under the curve (AUC), all presented with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). Heterogeneity among studies was assessed using the I2 statistic. The methodological quality of included studies was evaluated using a modified version of the Quality Assessment of Diagnostic Accuracy Studies-2 (QUADAS-2) tool.

Results

Of 918 identified studies, 32 studies with 3,709 cases were included. For the internal validation set, the pooled sensitivity, specificity, and AUC for detecting MVI in HCC were 0.83 (95% CI 0.79-0.87), 0.81 (95% CI 0.76-0.86), and 0.89 (95% CI 0.86-0.92), respectively. Radiologists achieved a sensitivity of 0.82 (95% CI 0.63-0.93), specificity of 0.65 (95% CI 0.45-0.81), and AUC of 0.80 (95% CI 0.77-0.84).

Conclusions

CT-based AI may have the potential to outperform radiologists in predicting MVI in HCC. However, existing evidence is limited by study heterogeneity and limited number of the direct comparison between AI and radiologists. Prospective multicenter studies are needed to validate its clinical utility.

records.title: A Decade of Artificial Intelligence in Stroke Care (2015-2025): Trends, Clinical Translation, and the Precision Medicine Frontier-A Narrative Review.

content.title: A Decade of Artificial Intelligence in Stroke Care (2015-2025): Trends, Clinical Translation, and the Precision Medicine Frontier-A Narrative Review.
content.abstract: Background/Objectives: Stroke generates 157 million disability-adjusted life-years (DALYs) annually, making it the leading neurological cause of global disease burden. Artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) have emerged as transformative technologies across the stroke care continuum. This narrative review maps the trajectory of AI in stroke medicine over the decade from 2015 to 2025. Methods: We conducted a narrative review with a structured, pre-specified search strategy across eight pre-specified thematic clusters using PubMed/MEDLINE (January 2015-December 2025), identifying 8549 records and including 1335 studies after screening. Inclusion criteria encompassed primary research articles, systematic reviews, meta-analyses, and RCTs reporting quantitative performance metrics or clinical outcome data for AI/ML in stroke. Results: Stroke imaging AI is the most commercially mature domain, with over 30 FDA-cleared tools. Automated ASPECTS scoring reduced radiologist reading time by 74.8% (AUC 84.97%; 95% CI: 83.1-86.8%). The only triage AI RCT demonstrated an 11.2 min reduction in door-to-groin time without significant improvement in 90-day functional independence (OR 1.3, 95% CI 0.42-4.0). Brain-computer interface rehabilitation showed significant upper limb recovery in a 17-center RCT (FMA-UE mean difference +3.35 points, 95% CI 1.05-5.65; p = 0.0045). AF detection AI is FDA-cleared and RCT-validated. LLMs and federated learning are pre-regulatory but growing exponentially. Conclusions: AI in stroke has achieved diagnostic maturity but therapeutic immaturity. Bridging algorithmic performance to patient outcomes, addressing equity gaps, and building the economic evidence base for scalable deployment are the defining challenges of the next decade.

records.title: The risk association between systemic lupus erythematosus and glaucoma: a systematic review and meta-analysis.

content.title: The risk association between systemic lupus erythematosus and glaucoma: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
content.abstract:
Background

Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE) is a systemic autoimmune disease that may damage multiple organs. About one-third of SLE patients have ocular manifestations. SLE as a potential risk factor for glaucoma has attracted attention, but existing study conclusions remain controversial. This meta-analysis aimed to evaluate the risk association between SLE and glaucoma and provide supportive evidence for the comorbidity follow-up of SLE patients.

Methods

The PubMed, EMBASE and Web of Science databases from the establishment of the database to November 2025 were retrieved, and studies measuring the association between SLE and glaucoma risk by hazard ratio (HR), odds ratio (OR), relative risk (RR), incidence rate ratio (IRR) and 95% confidence interval (CI) were included. Two researchers independently screened the literature, extracted the data and evaluated the risk of bias in the included studies. Meta-analysis was conducted using RevMan 5.3 software.

Results

Five cohort studies were included, involving 5516709 participants. Meta-analysis showed that SLE was associated with an increased risk of glaucoma (OR = 2.85, 95% CI: 1.26-6.47, P = 0.01). Subgroup analyses showed stronger associations in studies with fewer covariate adjustments and in those that did not adjust for corticosteroid use.

Conclusions

Existing evidence suggests that SLE may be associated with an increased risk of glaucoma. Given the limitations of this study, more prospective studies with rigorous design and full control of confounding factors are needed for further verification.

Systematic review registration

https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/prospero, identifier CRD420261303001.

records.title: Risk factors for diabetic kidney disease in type 2 diabetes mellitus in Asia: a meta-analysis.

content.title: Risk factors for diabetic kidney disease in type 2 diabetes mellitus in Asia: a meta-analysis.
content.abstract:
Background

Diabetic kidney disease (DKD) is a highly significant microvascular complication that arises from diabetes. Therefore, this study aimed to ascertain the traditional risk factors for DKD in type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) in Asia, raising awareness of these risk factors among patients with T2DM.

Methods

PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, and Cochrane Library were systematically searched until 13 Mar 2026. Case-control or cohort studies in Asia on the risk factors for DKD were included. Egger's test and funnel plots were used to assess publication bias. Stata 15 was used for statistical analysis.

Results

7 case-control studies (including 3,312 participants) and 17 cohort studies (including 8,735 participants) were included. All the included studies were of high quality according to the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale (NOS). Systolic blood pressure (SBP), hypertension, glycosylated hemoglobin (HbA1c), waist-to-hip ratio (WHR), fasting blood glucose (FBG), uric acid (UA), creatinine (Cr), age and diabetes duration were risk factors for DKD in T2DM. Diabetic retinopathy (DR) was closely associated with DKD, and this association was also evident in subgroups defined by pathological diagnosis. SBP was a risk factor in both the clinical diagnosis group and the pathological diagnosis group.

Conclusions

This meta-analysis preliminarily demonstrates that SBP, hypertension, HbA1c, WHR, FBG, UA, Cr, age, diabetes duration and DR are associated with DKD in Asia. SBP and DR are associated with renal biopsy-confirmed DKD.

Systematic review registration

https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/recorddashboard, identifier CRD42024529789.

records.title: Associations of metabolic score for insulin resistance with type 2 diabetes, cancer, and all-cause mortality: a meta-analysis of cohort studies.

content.title: Associations of metabolic score for insulin resistance with type 2 diabetes, cancer, and all-cause mortality: a meta-analysis of cohort studies.
content.abstract:
Objective

Insulin resistance (IR) constitutes a central pathophysiological mechanism underlying a spectrum of chronic metabolic disorders. The Metabolic Score for Insulin Resistance (METS-IR), which integrates fasting blood glucose (FBG), triglycerides (TG), high-density lipoprotein cholesterol (HDL-C), and body mass index (BMI), serves as a simple, cost-effective surrogate marker for IR. However, its associations with type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM), cancer, and all-cause mortality remain to be systematically synthesized. This study aims to systematically evaluate its clinical prognostic value.

Methods

We systematically searched PubMed, EMBASE, and Web of Science for prospective or retrospective cohort studies evaluating the associations of baseline METS-IR with incident T2DM, cancer, or all-cause mortality. Pooled hazard ratios (HRs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were calculated using random-effects models, and linear and nonlinear dose-response meta-analyses were performed. Heterogeneity, robustness, and publication bias were additionally assessed.

Results

A total of 23 cohort studies were included. For T2DM (6 studies), the highest METS-IR category was associated with a substantially elevated risk compared with the lowest category (HR = 4.03, 95% CI: 2.57-6.33), and per 1-standard deviation (1-SD) increment in METS-IR corresponded to a 48% higher risk (HR = 1.48, 95% CI: 1.24-1.77); dose-response analysis revealed a significant nonlinear increasing relationship (P for nonlinearity< 0.001). For cancer (5 studies), per 1-SD increment in METS-IR was associated with a 21% higher risk of cancer (HR = 1.21, 95% CI: 1.10-1.34); dose-response analysis indicated a significant nonlinear association (P for nonlinearity = 0.042). For all-cause mortality (13 studies), per 1-SD rise in METS-IR was linked to an 8% increased risk of all-cause death (HR = 1.08, 95% CI: 1.03-1.14); dose-response analysis demonstrated an overall linear increasing trend (P for linearity = 0.029), with each 20-unit increase in METS-IR associated with an approximately 2.8% higher risk of all-cause mortality (HR = 1.028, 95% CI: 1.004-1.056).

Conclusions

Elevated METS-IR levels are significantly associated with a nonlinear, progressive increase in the risk of incident T2DM. Its associations with cancer and all-cause mortality are weaker and more complex yet still exhibit consistent directional trends. METS-IR represents a convenient, readily applicable tool for early identification of metabolic risk using routine clinical parameters; however, its prognostic value for cancer and all-cause mortality merits further validation in large-scale, long-term follow-up studies.Systematic review registration: PROSPERO, identifier CRD420261293948.

records.title: Artificial Intelligence in Delirium Care: Predicting, Detecting, and Preventing Delirium in Older Hospitalized Adults.

content.title: Artificial Intelligence in Delirium Care: Predicting, Detecting, and Preventing Delirium in Older Hospitalized Adults.
content.abstract: Delirium is a common and serious complication of hospitalisation in older adults, but it is frequently missed because symptoms fluctuate, hypoactive presentations are subtle, and dementia complicates recognition of acute change. Artificial intelligence (AI), including machine learning, natural language processing (NLP), deep learning, and large language models, may support earlier risk stratification, enhanced surveillance, documentation review, and delivery of personalised prevention. This narrative review examines current evidence for AI in predicting, detecting, and preventing delirium in older hospitalised adults. It considers model development, external and temporal validation, calibration, clinical utility, workflow integration, frailty, dementia, multilingual documentation, explainability, fairness, privacy, and accountability. Existing studies show promising discrimination in retrospective datasets, and NLP can identify delirium-related information that is absent from diagnostic codes. However, performance often declines during external validation, calibration is inconsistently reported, and few systems have been tested prospectively in routine care. Established multicomponent non-pharmacological interventions remain the strongest evidence-based approach to prevention, while evidence that AI-triggered recommendations improve patient outcomes is limited. Future research should therefore move beyond technical accuracy toward prospective, multicentre, human-in-the-loop evaluations that measure alert burden, clinician response, intervention fidelity, patient-centred outcomes, and subgroup equity.

records.title: Perioperative neurofilament light chain and glial fibrillary acidic protein as biomarkers of postoperative delirium: a systematic review and meta-analysis.

content.title: Perioperative neurofilament light chain and glial fibrillary acidic protein as biomarkers of postoperative delirium: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
content.abstract:
Background

Postoperative delirium (POD) is a frequent and serious neurocognitive complication reflecting acute brain dysfunction and predicting long-term cognitive decline. Neurofilament light chain (NfL) and glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP) are biomarkers of neuronal and astroglial injury, but their relevance to POD remains uncertain.

Methods

This systematic review and meta-analysis aimed to determine whether there is an association between perioperative NfL or GFAP levels and POD. PubMed, Embase, and Web of Science were searched until January 2026. Odds ratios (ORs), standardized mean differences (SMDs), and diagnostic performance (AUC) were calculated using random-effects models.

Results

Fourteen studies involving 2,604 participants were included, of whom approximately 30% developed POD. In categorical analyses, higher NfL levels were associated with increased POD risk across nine studies (pooled OR = 1.27, 95% CI 1.08-1.50), consistent across plasma (OR = 1.27) and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) (OR = 1.32) samples. Continuous analyses also showed higher NfL concentrations in delirious patients (Plasma SMD = 0.48; CSF SMD = 0.40). GFAP showed a significant but weaker and less consistent association (overall OR = 1.68, 95% CI 1.15-2.43), mainly driven by plasma data, while continuous analyses were nonsignificant. Diagnostic meta-analysis showed fair discriminative performance for NfL (AUC = 0.68) and moderate accuracy for GFAP (AUC = 0.63).

Conclusions

This meta-analysis demonstrates that perioperative elevations of NfL and GFAP are associated with POD. However, their diagnostic performance remains modest, and current evidence does not support their use as stand-alone diagnostic biomarkers. NfL showed a more stable and reproducible relationship, suggesting its potential role as a marker of perioperative neural stress and as a component of future multimodal delirium risk models.

records.title: Efficacy and safety of obinutuzumab in refractory membranous nephropathy: a single-arm meta-analysis.

content.title: Efficacy and safety of obinutuzumab in refractory membranous nephropathy: a single-arm meta-analysis.
content.abstract:
Objective

Membranous nephropathy (MN) constitutes an autoimmune glomerular disorder and represents the most frequent etiology of primary nephrotic syndrome in adults. Although obinutuzumab exhibits favorable efficacy in managing refractory MN, outcomes diverge across individual investigations. Consequently, the present meta-analysis is undertaken to systematically evaluate the clinical efficacy and safety of obinutuzumab in individuals with refractory MN.

Methods

A systematic search was conducted across the Cochrane Library, Embase, Web of Science, and PubMed to determine relevant clinical investigations published up to November 12, 2025. Treatment effects were quantified employing the pooled proportion rate with 95% confidence interval (CI), mean difference (MD, 95% CI), and standardized mean difference (SMD, 95% CI). Heterogeneity was examined via the I² statistic. Subgroup analyses were implemented based on the geographic distribution of the study population and duration of follow-up. All extracted data were subjected to statistical analysis using R (v4.5.2).

Results

The present meta-analysis ultimately incorporated 12 articles (222 individuals) after applying the eligibility criteria. Concerning remission rates, the overall clinical remission rate reached 86% (95% CI: 80% to 90%), the complete clinical remission rate stood at 31% (25% to 37%), the partial clinical remission rate was 55% (49% to 63%), and the immunologic remission rate achieved 88% (81% to 92%). Obinutuzumab reduced proteinuria (SMD = -1.2, 95%CI -1.37 to -1.03) and raised serum albumin (MD = 12.5, 95%CI 9.91-15.08), while eGFR showed no significant change (MD = 3.23, 95%CI -3.76-10.21). The pooled adverse event rate was 29% (95%CI 15%-48%), with two fatal pneumonia-related events: severe COVID-19 pneumonia and pneumonia-induced respiratory failure.

Conclusion

Obinutuzumab demonstrates marked efficacy in treating refractory MN, with an overall clinical remission rate of 86% and a low incidence of severe adverse events. This profile signifies a potential therapeutic role for this condition. However, all raw data included in this meta-analysis were derived from uncontrolled retrospective single-arm trials and case series. Given factors such as selection bias, the remission rate may be overestimated. Large-scale, multicenter randomized controlled trials are necessary for verification in future investigations.

Systematic review registration

https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/, identifier CRD420251231344.

records.title: Artificial intelligence in the diagnosis and identification of bacterial pathogens: Current advances and future perspectives.

content.title: Artificial intelligence in the diagnosis and identification of bacterial pathogens: Current advances and future perspectives.
content.abstract: Bacterial infections remain a major global health challenge, which are responsible for significant morbidity, mortality, and increasing antimicrobial resistance worldwide. Rapid and accurate identification of bacterial pathogens is therefore essential for guiding appropriate antimicrobial therapy, improving patient outcomes, and supporting effective infection control strategies. However, conventional microbiological diagnostic methods such as culture, microscopy, and biochemical testing are often time-consuming, labor-intensive, and dependent on expert interpretation. In recent years, artificial intelligence (AI) has increasingly emerged as a powerful tool capable of transforming clinical microbiology by enabling rapid analysis of complex biomedical data. This review aims to provide a comprehensive overview of the role of AI in the diagnosis and identification of bacterial pathogens and to discuss its current applications, advantages, limitations, and future perspectives. Key AI-assisted technologies, including machine learning and deep learning algorithms such as Random Forest, Support Vector Machines, Artificial Neural Networks, and Convolutional Neural Networks, are increasingly applied to diagnostic platforms, including automated microscopy, next-generation genomic sequencing, MALDI-TOF mass spectrometry, and clinical data analysis systems. Current evidence indicates that AI-assisted diagnostic approaches can substantially improve the speed, accuracy, and automation of microbial pathogen detection while enabling large-scale analysis of microbiological and clinical datasets. In the future, AI-integrated microbiology laboratories, rapid diagnostic platforms, genomic surveillance systems, and AI-assisted clinical decision support tools are expected to further enhance infectious disease diagnostics and contribute to improved antimicrobial stewardship and global infection management.

records.title: Artificial intelligence applications in CBCT-based assessment of craniofacial airway volume and shape in sleep-disordered breathing: a systematic review.

content.title: Artificial intelligence applications in CBCT-based assessment of craniofacial airway volume and shape in sleep-disordered breathing: a systematic review.
content.abstract:
Background

Sleep-disordered breathing (SDB), including obstructive sleep apnea (OSA), is strongly influenced by craniofacial airway morphology. Cone-beam computed tomography (CBCT) enables three-dimensional airway assessment; however, manual segmentation is time-consuming and subject to variability. Artificial intelligence (AI) has emerged as a potential tool to automate airway analysis. This systematic review evaluates the technical performance and clinical applicability of AI in CBCT-based craniofacial airway assessment for SDB.

Methods

This review was conducted in accordance with PRISMA 2020 guidelines and prospectively registered in PROSPERO (CRD 420251065028). A comprehensive search of PubMed, Ovid, Scopus, and Google Scholar was performed for studies published from 2015 onward. Eligibility criteria included diagnostic or validation studies assessing AI-based CBCT airway segmentation, landmark detection, or OSA prediction. Dual independent screening was conducted, and risk of bias was assessed using QUADAS-2.

Results

Fourteen studies met the inclusion criteria. Most implemented deep learning architectures, particularly convolutional neural networks-based models such as U-Net and SpatialConfiguration-Net. Reported Dice Similarity Coefficients ranged from 0.90 to 0.97, and intraclass correlation coefficients for volumetric measurements typically exceeded 0.90, indicating strong agreement with manual segmentation. AI systems substantially reduced annotation time compared with manual methods. However, heterogeneity was considerable across AI architectures, anatomical targets, datasets, and outcome metrics. External validation was limited, and only one study evaluated OSA prediction against polysomnography.

Conclusions

AI demonstrates high technical accuracy and efficiency in CBCT-based airway segmentation and morphometric analysis. Nevertheless, current evidence largely reflects internal technical validation rather than confirmed clinical utility. Additional prospective, multicenter studies incorporating clinical outcome validation are required before routine clinical implementation can be fully supported.

records.title: Prevalence and associated factors of gestational diabetes mellitus among women with polycystic ovary syndrome: a systematic review and meta-analysis.

content.title: Prevalence and associated factors of gestational diabetes mellitus among women with polycystic ovary syndrome: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
content.abstract:
Objective

Polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS), the most common endocrine disorder in reproductive-aged women, often leads to gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM). This study aimed to systematically evaluate GDM prevalence and its associated factors in PCOS.

Methods

We searched PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, Cochrane Library, CNKI, Wanfang, Sinomed, and VIP from inception to December 31, 2025. Studies reporting GDM prevalence or associated factors in PCOS were included. A random-effects model pooled prevalence with odds ratios. Egger's test assessed publication bias, and subgroup analysis with meta-regression explored heterogeneity. A logit transformation was applied for pooling.

Results

Twenty-two studies with 5,507 PCOS patients were included. The pooled GDM prevalence was 24% (95% CI: 20%-28%; prediction interval: 10%-46%), with substantial heterogeneity (I² = 89.9%). The primary prevalence estimate, based on cohort studies (n=13), was 21.7% (95% CI: 17.7%-25.8%), while the overall estimate including case-control studies was 24% (95% CI: 20%-28%). By diagnostic criteria, GDM prevalence was 26.0% for one-step vs. 18.7% for two-step. Potentially associated factors included pre-pregnancy BMI (OR = 1.39), gestational weight gain (OR = 1.58), HOMA-IR (OR = 3.41), and family history of diabetes (OR = 2.88).

Conclusion

Although the pooled GDM prevalence in PCOS was 24%, substantial heterogeneity and a wide prediction interval (10%-46%) suggest the true prevalence varies considerably across settings. Associated factors included HOMA-IR, family history, pre-pregnancy overweight, and excessive gestational weight gain. PCOS patients should be considered a high-risk group, and early monitoring of glucose metabolism and weight management may be beneficial, though these recommendations derive from observed rather than interventional evidence.

Systematic review registration

https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/view/CRD42026128476, identifier: CRD420261284765.

records.title: Risk factors for post-COVID-19 condition among previously hospitalized COVID-19 patients: a systematic review and meta-analysis.

content.title: Risk factors for post-COVID-19 condition among previously hospitalized COVID-19 patients: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
content.abstract:
Background

Post-COVID-19 condition is a major source of long-term morbidity after SARS-CoV-2 infection. Patients hospitalized for COVID-19 may be at particularly high risk because hospitalization often reflects greater acute disease severity and comorbidity burden. However, evidence on risk factors in previously hospitalized populations remains inconsistent due to differences in outcome definitions, follow-up periods, and analytical approaches. This systematic review and meta-analysis aimed to identify risk factors associated with post-COVID outcomes among patients previously hospitalized for COVID-19.

Methods

A systematic review and meta-analysis was conducted following PRISMA 2020 principles. PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, Web of Science Core Collection, and the WHO COVID-19 Global Literature Database were searched for studies published between 1 January 2020 and 24 February 2026. Eligible studies included hospitalized patients with confirmed or probable COVID-19, assessed post-acute outcomes at least 4 weeks after acute infection, hospitalization, recovery, or discharge, and evaluated at least one candidate risk factor. Adjusted effect estimates were prioritized, and random-effects meta-analyses were performed when at least two comparable estimates were available.

Results

Eleven studies were included in the qualitative synthesis, and seven contributed to quantitative meta-analysis. Five risk-factor groups were pooled: female sex, acute disease severity or respiratory support, intensive care unit (ICU) admission, vaccination status, and hypertension. Female sex was associated with higher odds of post-COVID outcomes (OR 1.94, 95% CI 1.60-2.35; I 2 = 6.9%). The strongest association was observed for greater acute disease severity or advanced respiratory support (OR 2.55, 95% CI 1.77-3.68; I 2 = 13.0%). ICU admission (OR 1.88, 95% CI 1.24-2.83), no or incomplete vaccination (OR 1.90, 95% CI 1.33-2.72), and hypertension (OR 1.60, 95% CI 1.16-2.20) were also associated with increased odds. Additional predictors, including obesity, age, smoking, dysgeusia, symptom burden, and neurological or psychiatric comorbidity, were summarized narratively.

Conclusion

Among previously hospitalized COVID-19 patients, the most consistent risk factors for post-COVID outcomes were female sex, greater acute disease severity or respiratory support, ICU admission, no or incomplete vaccination, and hypertension. These findings support risk-based post-discharge follow-up, although the evidence remains limited by heterogeneous outcome definitions and the small number of studies available for several risk factors.

records.title: Diagnostic Accuracy of Artificial Intelligence in Detecting Pleural Effusion on Ultrasound Imaging: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.

content.title: Diagnostic Accuracy of Artificial Intelligence in Detecting Pleural Effusion on Ultrasound Imaging: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
content.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) interpretation of ultrasound (US) images is promising, yet its accuracy in diagnosing pleural effusions remains unclear. We conducted a comprehensive database search which identified 84 studies, of which 6 met eligibility criteria. We included 2951 patients with 58 392 images and 12 069 ultrasound clips. Bivariate analysis revealed a pooled sensitivity of 0.92 (95% CI: 0.85-0.96, p < 0.05) and specificity of 0.96 (95% CI: 0.88-0.99, p < 0.05), with a high AUC of 0.98 under the sROC curve, although included studies had significant heterogeneity, I <sup>2</sup> > 99%. AI demonstrates high diagnostic accuracy in detecting pleural effusion on ultrasound.

records.title: Barriers to Clinical Integration of Artificial Intelligence in Computer-Assisted Dental Implant Surgery: A Critical Review.
records.publisher: Oral and maxillofacial surgery clinics of North America

content.title: Barriers to Clinical Integration of Artificial Intelligence in Computer-Assisted Dental Implant Surgery: A Critical Review.
content.abstract: Translating artificial intelligence (AI) from virtual implant planning to dental implant surgical execution is obstructed by technical, clinical, and socioethical barriers. This critical review appraises these impediments, focusing on tomographic data heterogeneity, closed hardware ecosystems that block kinematic data extraction, and algorithmic opacity that erodes clinician trust. Current literature over-relies on static retrospective validations with high bias risk. This gap should be bridged by a roadmap prioritizing federated learning, open-source interoperability, explainable AI, and prospective multicenter trials to establish algorithms as dynamically adaptive surgical systems.

records.title: Artificial intelligence in acute stroke imaging: A comprehensive survey from imaging assessment to outcome prediction.
records.publisher: Computerized medical imaging and graphics : the official journal of the Computerized Medical Imaging Society

content.title: Artificial intelligence in acute stroke imaging: A comprehensive survey from imaging assessment to outcome prediction.
content.abstract: Acute strokes encompass two main types: acute ischemic stroke (AIS) and intracerebral hemorrhage (ICH). Each type involves specific imaging techniques and entails different clinical considerations. While deep learning has facilitated the analysis of stroke imaging autonomously, the technical differences between these two stroke types have not been examined within a shared analytical framework. This review addresses that gap through the examination of 84 peer-reviewed articles. A PRISMA-compliant search was conducted using multiple databases. Analysis of the ICH pipeline predominantly uses CT imaging and is primarily centered on a classification task. The main focus is on hemorrhage identification, subtype classification, hematoma expansion prediction, and forecasting associated clinical outcomes. The AIS pipeline is primarily based on quantification and therefore uses a variety of imaging techniques to optimize and automate the analysis of a specific set of clinical questions related to the stroke. Core tasks include segmentation of the infarct area, assessment scoring, large vessel occlusion, core-penumbra mismatch analysis, and prediction of outcomes. Convergence is also observed in outcome prediction approaches across both domains. Existing models demonstrate clinically acceptable performance across numerous tasks. Clinical deployment nonetheless remains limited by the lack of external validation, high costs of annotation, demands of real-time processing, and poor prospective evidence. This review offers practical guidance to develop fully operational AI systems that can be integrated into emergency stroke care.

records.title: MRI-Based Radiomics and Artificial Intelligence for Prediction of Recurrence and Prognostic Outcomes in Oral Tongue Squamous Cell Carcinoma: A Systematic Review with Functional Meta-Synthesis.

content.title: MRI-Based Radiomics and Artificial Intelligence for Prediction of Recurrence and Prognostic Outcomes in Oral Tongue Squamous Cell Carcinoma: A Systematic Review with Functional Meta-Synthesis.
content.abstract:
Background/objectives

Oral tongue squamous cell carcinoma (OTSCC) remains clinically challenging because conventional clinicopathological markers do not fully explain variability in recurrence and survival. This systematic review and functional meta-synthesis aimed to identify and critically appraise studies using preoperative magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)-based radiomics, artificial intelligence (AI), deep learning, or quantitative MRI-derived models to predict recurrence and prognostic outcomes in OTSCC.

Methods

PubMed, Scopus, and Embase were searched from inception to March 2026. Eligible studies included prognostic model investigations in adults with OTSCC or primary tongue cancer without reported base-of-tongue/oropharyngeal involvement, undergoing preoperative MRI and surgery, with recurrence- or survival-related follow-up. The primary synthesis was a functional meta-synthesis; pooling was not performed because studies were not sufficiently comparable.

Results

Seven retrospective studies were included, with a summed descriptive sample of 1287 participants. The evidence base was heterogeneous in MRI sequences, segmentation workflows, model architecture, validation strategy, and endpoint definition. Functional meta-synthesis identified four domains: direct recurrence-oriented modeling, broader prognostic stratification, reported incremental or complementary value over clinical frameworks, and translational maturity/technical implementation. Several studies reported associations between MRI-derived signatures and recurrence- or survival-related outcomes, but findings were interpreted narratively because of differences in primary endpoints, imaging features, model design, validation methods, and outcome definitions. Most studies were judged at high overall risk of bias, and certainty of evidence ranged from low to very low.

Conclusions

MRI-based radiomics and AI show preliminary promise for prognostic stratification in OTSCC, particularly recurrence-related risk refinement, but current evidence remains limited by retrospective design, heterogeneity, sparse external validation, and low certainty.

records.title: The value of chest CT in the differential diagnosis of benign and malignant pulmonary nodules: a meta-analysis.

content.title: The value of chest CT in the differential diagnosis of benign and malignant pulmonary nodules: a meta-analysis.
content.abstract:
Background

This study was conducted to systematically evaluate the diagnostic value of computed tomography (CT) in differentiating benign and malignant pulmonary nodules through a meta-analysis, thereby providing a solid evidence-based foundation for clinical diagnosis and treatment decisions.

Methods

We searched the PubMed, Web of Science, Embase, Medline, China National Knowledge Infrastructure (CNKI), and Cochrane Library databases for relevant studies published up to December 2025 and performed a meta-analysis using Review Manager v.5.4.

Results

A total of 28 retrospective analyses and 19 prospective studies were included, comprising 4,705 patients with pulmonary nodules. The pooled sensitivity of CT was 0.90 (95% confidence interval [CI]: 0.89-0.91; p < 0.001), while the pooled specificity was 0.74 (95% CI: 0.72-0.76; p < 0.001). The positive likelihood ratio was 3.28 (95% CI: 2.81-3.83; p < 0.001), the negative likelihood ratio was 0.13 (95% CI: 0.10-0.17; p < 0.001), and the diagnostic odds ratio (DOR) was 33.20 (95% CI: 23.52-46.87; p < 0.001). The area under the summary receiver operating characteristic (SROC) curve was 0.9177.

Conclusion

These findings indicate that CT has a high diagnostic value in differentiating benign from malignant pulmonary nodules and is an important method for evaluating pulmonary nodules in clinical practice.

Systematic review registration

https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/view/CRD420261277036, Identifier: CRD420261277036.

records.title: Immune checkpoint inhibitors plus trastuzumab and chemotherapy for the treatment of advanced HER2-positive gastric and gastroesophageal junction cancers: a systematic review and meta-analysis.

content.title: Immune checkpoint inhibitors plus trastuzumab and chemotherapy for the treatment of advanced HER2-positive gastric and gastroesophageal junction cancers: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
content.abstract:
Background

HER2-positive gastric and gastroesophageal junction (GEJ) cancers have poor prognosis despite standard trastuzumab-based chemotherapy. Immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) may enhance therapeutic efficacy when combined with trastuzumab.

Methods
